#### Why choosing session windows adds two components and a storage requirement

**The question.** Design session-window analytics for user activity. A late event can change a session that was already emitted, so the pipeline must retract the stale pane rather than double-count.

**The pipeline:** event source → window assigner → **session merger** → keyed session state → **trigger / retraction emitter** → analytics store.

Two of those six stages exist **only** because a session's bounds can change after the fact: the merger and the retraction emitter. So "we'll use session windows" is not a configuration change — it adds two components and places a hard requirement on the store.

**Two examples, kept apart.** The component bullets above drop the keys, treat all 9 events as one user's, and use the interview section's G = 47s: there id 7 **bridges** two sessions, so panes 8 and 9 are retracted and 21 is emitted. Everything from here on uses the **keyed** stream (keys a and b) at the book's gap of 120s and at 40s, where id 7 only ever meets key "b"'s sessions and **extends** one instead of bridging two. Every figure below belongs to the keyed stream.

**The requirement, stated precisely.** At gap 40s this stream produces: session [12:01:30, 12:01:30] ids 2 sum 7 emitted at event 4, so the store holds 7. Then id 7 arrives at event 7 and the session becomes [12:00:50, 12:01:30] ids 7,2 sum 11. The emitter must retract 7 **for the old bounds** and emit 11 for the new ones. A store that ignores the retraction reads 18 for a session worth 11.

Note what makes this harder than a fixed window's correction: the retraction names the **old bounds**. A fixed window's correction updates a row; a session's correction **deletes one row and inserts another**, because the bounds are the key.

**And the two settings are coupled.** Gap 120s gives key a 3 sessions and needs 0 retractions; gap 40s gives 4 sessions and needs 1. A smaller gap means more sessions **and** earlier collection, and earlier collection is what creates the retraction.

#### When this design is viable, and the four things it does not settle

**It is viable when the analytics store can delete a row.** That is the first thing to check, before any of the rest: a key-value store or a warehouse with upsert-and-delete is fine; an append-only event log or a billing ledger is not, and no amount of pipeline work fixes it.

**Choose the gap as a product definition, then accept its consequences.** It decides how many sessions exist AND whether retractions are required. Those are not independent knobs, and the second one reaches into the storage contract.

**Set allowed lateness against the memory, not against the skew.** It is how long past end + gap a session's state is kept so a late event can still revive it (this chapter sets none, so every figure above uses end + gap), so it is the price of being able to correct — paid in bytes per open (key, session) pair.

**What this design does NOT settle — four gaps:**

1. **Session state is data-dependent.** 5 entries for 9 events in the keyed stream at gap 120s (the one-user example at G = 47s ends with 3), and nothing bounds it for a burstier stream or a larger key space. Fixed windows can be sized in advance; this cannot.
2. **One session is never collected**, because the watermark never reaches 12:11:00. Its state is held for the life of the job regardless of allowed lateness — a low-traffic key is a permanent allocation.
3. **The bridge case is not demonstrated in this keyed stream.** This stream's late event extends a session; one that merged two already-published sessions would retract two panes and emit one. Same mechanism, twice the bookkeeping, and no event in this keyed stream does it at gap 120s or 40s. The Google Interview Question section shows it on the same event times with the keys dropped and G = 47s: arrival 50 withdraws 1..3 and 90..130 and replaces them with 1..130.
4. **The gap is unverifiable.** Every session count stated for the book's gap is correct for 120s and for no other definition — the same stream gives 4, 3, 2, 1 sessions for key a at 40s, 120s, 130s, 300s — and nothing in the data can tell you whether 120s is the right definition of a visit.

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch04-system/frames/step-01.svg" alt="Step 1: the pipeline, and the stage that only sessions need" width="1040">

Name what sessions cost before designing with them. The merger and the retraction emitter have no equivalent in a fixed-window pipeline, and the analytics store acquires a hard requirement: it must accept a retraction. A store that can only append is not compatible with session windows at all, and that is discovered late if it is not named here.

<details>
<summary><b>Step 2 of 4</b> — the retraction, with real values</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch04-system/frames/step-02.svg" alt="Step 2: the retraction, with real values" width="1040">

The sharp detail is in the note: a fixed window's correction updates a row, and a session's correction **deletes one row and inserts another**, because the session's bounds are its identity. A store keyed by (key, session start) cannot express that as an update — and a pipeline that emits only the new value leaves the old row behind, reading 18 where 11 is right.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 3 of 4</b> — the two settings that decide the whole design</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch04-system/frames/step-03.svg" alt="Step 3: the two settings that decide the whole design" width="1040">

The coupling in the note is the thing to take away. Shrinking the gap from 120s to 40s changes key a from 3 to 4 sessions — and simultaneously makes 1 retraction mandatory, because sessions now close before the straggler lands. A product decision about what counts as a visit reaches into the storage contract.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 4 of 4</b> — and what this design does NOT settle</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch04-system/frames/step-04.svg" alt="Step 4: and what this design does NOT settle" width="1040">

The third note is worth stating plainly rather than implying: this dataset's straggler extends one session, so the bridge case — one event merging two already-published sessions — is not demonstrated in this keyed stream. It is the same retraction mechanism applied twice. The Google Interview Question section shows it on the same event times with the keys dropped and G = 47s: arrival 50 withdraws 1..3 and 90..130 and replaces them with 1..130.

</details>
